Drawings, posters, watercolours, photos, prints, etchings or lithographs - everything you ever wanted to know about the graphic arts but were afraid to ask, you'll find here!

Everything you've always wanted to know about graphic arts but never dared to ask is here! Derived from the Greek word graphein (to write), graphic arts refer to all technical processes (drawing, printmaking, graphic design...) used in the visual conception or presentation of an artwork. By extension, they include all image reproduction methods, such as photography. In online graphic art auctions, you’ll find posters, drawings in watercolor, gouache or graphite on paper. These sheets, old or contemporary, where the art of line competes with prints — images reproduced from engraved or drawn supports: engravings, lithographs, silkscreens, etc. The aim is to make an impression. Graphic art sales also give prominence to photography, from albumen paper prints by Gustave Le Gray, Brassaï, Doisneau, Robert Capa, to contemporary works by Nan Goldin or the Magnum agency — even to pieces by street artists whose tags, stencils, and graffiti have moved from the streets to auction rooms and online sales. Did you know? A fake £10 note created by Banksy and handed out for free to the Notting Hill crowd in 2004 can now fetch sky-high prices at Hôtel Drouot. Kaws, Invader, Jonone are also in the spotlight. Assembled far from the spotlight, bucking prevailing trends, this collection was built with a rare freedom of vision. While some of its pieces had previously been shown to the public in exhibitions, the collection assembled by Liliane and Michel Durand-Dessert had never before been revealed in its entirety. What Millon is presenting today is therefore not merely an auction: it is the discovery of a collector’s journey, pursued for more than thirty years within one of the Himalayas’ least understood artistic worlds.

For the Himalayas occupy a unique place in the history of Western taste for primitive arts: that of one of the last territories to remain largely unexplored. While Africa, Oceania, and pre-Columbian America had long had their connoisseurs, dealers, and scholarly circles, the high valleys of Nepal remained a blind spot—a land of legend rather than of collecting, known to travelers but still largely unknown to art lovers. It was amid this silence that this adventure began in the late 1980s, driven by the conviction that these objects deserved to be viewed for what they were: not ethnographic curiosities, but works of art in their own right.
The Heights of Himalayan Art - The Liliane & Michel Durand Dessert Collection
